extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline, and disciplinary enforcement authorities
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements used by the USPTO to evaluate and discipline patent practitioners, including applicable CFR provisions, practitioner duties (timeliness, client notification, supervision), settlement-agreement requirements, and sanctions such as public reprimand and publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement Agreement requirements under 37 C.F.R. § 11.26
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Settlement Agreement must set forth stipulated facts, legal conclusions, and sanctions to which the parties have agreed, and satisfy the requirements of 37 C.F.R. § 11.26 in order to resolve disciplinary action voluntarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order reflects the parties' stipulated facts, legal conclusions, and agreed-upon discipline pursuant to the Proposed Settlement Agreement; satisfying § 11.26 is a prerequisite for acceptance of such settlements by the Director.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Director jurisdiction (statutory/ regulatory basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction over practitioner discipline pursuant to 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32, and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.20(a)(3) and 11.26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory and regulatory citations provide the authority to adjudicate discipline and to issue Final Orders resolving disciplinary matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) — conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding that a practitioner's actions interfered with administration of justice supports discipline under this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6) — conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes engaging in conduct that adversely reflects upon a practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct that undermines confidence in a practitioner's ability to practice before the USPTO may be disciplined under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8) — failure to notify client of significant Office correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes failing to notify a client of correspondence received from the Office when the correspondence could have a significant effect upon the matter pending before the Office, is received by the practitioner on behalf of the client, and is correspondence a reasonable practitioner would believe the client should be notified of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Notices of Missing Parts; failing to inform the client of such correspondence (and resulting consequences like abandonment) is a basis for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) — neglect of a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to act (timely filings, status inquiries, client communication) on matters for which the practitioner is responsible constitutes neglect under this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to respond timely to Notices of Missing Parts and file required items
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Office issues Notices of Missing Parts (e.g., missing basic filing fee, unsigned oath/declaration), the practitioner must file all required items within the prescribed time period (the notices here gave two months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to timely submit required filing fees and signed oaths/declarations can lead to abandonment of applications and support disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that filings be properly signed and dated
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents submitted (requests for extensions, declarations, responses) must be properly signed and dated; unsigned or undated documents or documents dated earlier but filed later may be treated as untimely or invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision cites filings purporting to be signed March 10 but filed June 6 and the Office treating the June filings as untimely; proper execution and dating are essential to preserve filing rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify client of practitioner actions, status changes, and cessation of representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must notify the client of actions taken on the client's behalf, any cessation of acting for the client, changes in status of applications (such as abandonment), and changes in contact information (relocation of practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to notify the client of abandonment or of a change of address contributed to discipline in this case; client notification is a required professional responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to ensure continuity and to identify matters of primary responsibility when leaving a firm
rubrics_metrics.description: When a practitioner leaves a firm, they must identify matters for which they bear primary responsibility and take steps to ensure those matters are properly handled and that the client is informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The respondent's failure to identify matters for which she bore primary responsibility upon departure contributed to neglect and was cited as misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to inquire about and monitor the status of pending matters with the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should make further inquiries of the Office regarding the status of matters they have filed and are responsible for, rather than ceasing contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After last filings on June 7, 2006, there was no further contact from respondent; lack of inquiry about status is part of neglectful conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors considered in determining discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors such as disorganized, fragmented, or fractious business relationships among attorneys and administrative oversight problems may be considered mitigating when assessing sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order notes the respondent's disorganized practice relationships as mitigating; mitigating factors can influence the agreed sanctions or severity of discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice of discipline per 37 C.F.R. § 11.59
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall publish Final Orders and give notice of public discipline and reasons to disciplinary enforcement agencies in the states where the practitioner is admitted, to courts where admitted, and to the public, including publication in the Official Gazette and posting in the OED Reading Room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public reprimand and publication are mandatory consequences under § 11.59 for certain disciplinary resolutions; the order includes the required Official Gazette notice text and posting instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible sanctions and cost allocation in settlement orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies for violations may include public reprimand, publication of the order, notice to other disciplinary bodies, and agreement on allocation of costs; parties may agree each will bear their own costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this case the agreed sanction was a public reprimand, publication of the Final Order and Official Gazette notice, notice to disciplinary agencies, and each party bearing its own costs.
